disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, often accompanied by depressive episodes, with mood and energy changes that are clearly distinct from the person's usual functioning and cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. Manic episodes typically involve persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity or energy lasting at least one week, though episodes can last months if untreated. The course is usually recurrent, with episodes triggered or unmasked by stressors, sleep disruption, or substance use, but not solely caused by them. It is distinguished from Bipolar II by the presence of full mania (rather than hypomania) and from unipolar depression or primary psychotic disorders by the cyclical pattern of mood elevation and depression and the temporal relationship between mood and psychotic features when present.

narrative.stressor: Alfred’s first clear manic episode emerged over the seven months after he took on a demanding new role: studying nights for his Master Electrician exam while working overtime on a large commercial solar and home-automation contract. Initially, his family appreciated his extra drive and long hours in the garage planning a future family-run business, but as the project grew, he began insisting on expanding the scope, volunteering his small crew for unpaid extras, and pushing unsafe timelines that alarmed his supervisor. At home, his wife noticed that he stopped coming to Sunday barbecues and softball because he was constantly starting new side jobs and DIY electronics projects he refused to abandon, and their finances became strained when he unilaterally ordered expensive tools and solar inventory on credit for a business that didn’t yet exist. The breaking point came when a major customer complained about chaotic scheduling and Alfred’s increasingly confrontational, "wired" demeanor on-site, prompting his employer to pull him from field work; his wife, worried about his drastic change and inability to slow down or sleep, brought him to a psychiatrist after his apprenticeship mentees reported being scared by his intensity.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to slow down—I’m constantly taking on new projects and working nonstop, like I’m stuck in overdrive.”

narrative.stressor: Martha’s episode developed during a high-stakes year when she secured a major grant and was promoted to lead a new condensed matter lab, coinciding with a heavy teaching load and several grant deadlines. At first, colleagues saw her as simply energized and productive, staying late to run experiments and sending an unusual volume of late-night emails, but over several months her intensity escalated as she proposed multiple new projects, demanded round-the-clock availability from students, and began rewriting approved protocols on the fly. Her meticulous planning gave way to chaotic, overambitious commitments: she volunteered to organize a regional conference, agreed to extra committee work, and insisted on reanalyzing years’ worth of data, leading to missed deadlines, complaints from graduate students, and concern from department leadership about her increasingly volatile meetings. After a tense faculty review where she reacted angrily to feedback and her partner at home reported that she hadn’t been sleeping and seemed uncharacteristically “amped up” and distractible, her department chair privately suggested she see occupational health, which then referred her for psychiatric evaluation when it became clear her work and relationships were significantly impaired.
narrative.chief_complaint: “For months I’ve felt unusually ‘up’ and on edge all the time, like my mood is cranked way higher than normal and I can’t dial it back.”

narrative.stressor: Daniel’s symptoms became clinically significant during a transition from long-haul driving into a regional freight sales role, a move he hoped would give him more time at home and open a path toward coordinating or training. The new position brought a mix of freedom and pressure: looser structure, commission-based income, and expectations to build his own client list, which initially seemed invigorating as he threw himself into networking, early-morning prospecting drives for sunrise photos, and ambitious plans for side woodworking and photography businesses. Over the next seven months, his family and coworkers noticed he was increasingly preoccupied with big, shifting plans, spending long hours on the road chasing leads and gear purchases, missing family obligations, and clashing with his manager when questioned about erratic schedules and overpromising to clients. After a near loss of a key account due to his disorganized follow-through and an argument at home about mounting credit card debt from photography and woodworking equipment, Daniel—already reading about mental health for his anxiety—agreed to see a psychiatrist when he realized he couldn’t keep his mind on one task long enough to do his new job reliably.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps jumping to every little thing around me, and I can’t stay focused on what I’m supposed to be doing anymore.”
